newsitem.title: UK: Ex-UK air cargo rates firm,strong demand to end 96.
newsitem.headline: Ex-UK air cargo rates firm,strong demand to end 96.

text.p: Ex-UK air cargo rates are steady to marginally firmer driven by strong demand for capacity to most destinations, a Reuters survey shows.

The level of demand reflects both a seasonal fourth quarter upturn in air cargo volumes, but also the continued high growth in UK exports. Airlines are still keen to maintain yields rather simply raise underlying tariffs, air cargo industry sources said.

The decision by a number of European carriers, including Deutsche Lufthansa, KLM Royal Dutch Airlines NV Swissair and Air France, to introduce cargo fuel surcharges or rate increases to compensate for sharply higher jet fuel costs had no immediate pact on market sentiment.
Virgin Atlantic is also introducing a surcharge from November 4, while North American airlines have adopted a "wait and see" attitude on fuel surcharges.
Most airlines operating between Hong Kong and Europe are planning an HK80 cents a kg surcharge from November 4, and a similar charge is expected on transpacific routes from Hong Kong.

The situation has become sufficiently serious for the International Air Transport Association (IATA) to call an emergency meeting for November 13 to discuss the impact of rising fuel costs on member airlines.

Average rates to Tokyo were around 2.06 stg a kg for 100 kgs compared to the previous 2.05 stg, with Seoul at 1.97 stg a kg against 1.95 stg. Hong Kong moved to 1.22 stg a kg from 1.20 stg, with the average to Singapore also gaining to 1.28 stg from 1.26 stg. Sydney moved to 2.12 stg a kg from 2.10 stg with some quotes as high as 2.30 stg.
North east Asia remains the strongest air freight market out of the UK with business described as "buoyant and booming".

Tony Edwards, cargo manager for Japan Airlines said," the forecasts are very good. Basically all the cargo space is taken for November and December and any space capacity will be used by seasonal mail shipments."

"Yields have improved slightly. Business is steady," added Frank Smith from Korean Airlines Ltd. Volumes to Seoul have been at high levels in recent months, a reflection of the increasing trade and investment links between Britain and South Korea.
For Cathay Pacific Airways Ltd the "Hong Kong market is booming, with business to Australia also really good" said cargo sales executive James Gilliard.

"Yields are being maintained with space fully booked three to four days in advance," he added. There is good demand for Korea, while business to Japan is limited by capacity available out of Hong Kong."
Martin Friend from Singapore Airlines said," the past three weeks have been as busy as they can be with bookings at high levels. We hope this will continue to the end of the year."

To the United States, average rates were slightly firmer at around 0.63 stg a kg per 100 kgs to JFK against a previous 0.62 stg, although some current quotes are as low for 0.40 a kg for some shipments, industry sources said.
To Los Angeles and Chicago average rates were steady at around 0.73 stg and 0.72 stg respectively.

Despite recent traffic being hit by transatlantic storms affecting both fuel and capacity, "I'm hopeful that if November and December are as good as October has been, then we'll finish the year better than I anticipated," said American Airlines cargo manager, John Smith.
"Volumes are holding and yields doing very well," he added. "The rise in the value of the pound has provided a minor currency benefit as our remittances are in dollar," Smith said.
However, sterling's present value of around US$1.60 is "probably just about right" and anything stronger might hit British exports to the U.S., he added.
"And once the U.S. election is out of the way, we'll have a better idea of U.S. consumer attitudes and whether they propose to start spending or back off," Smith said.
At United Airlines, UK cargo manager, Peter Chase described "business as not bad" and said the last quarter traditional recovery was underway.
"We hope it will got through to the end of the year," he said.
"Air cargo rates are steady. There is no pressure them up but neither is there any to push them down," Chase added.

The latest available data from airlines and members of the British International Freight Association (BIFA) confirmed that volumes to North America were starting to climb in August and September, said BIFA's Roger Blacklock and that the trend is continuing.

Rates to the Middle East are firming, despite competition. The average is now around 0.85 stg a kg for a 100 kgs to Dubai, compared to 0.80 stg previously but quality carriers can charge more than the one stg level. Bahrain is nudging upwards to around 0.98 stg a kg from the earlier 0.85 stg.

Seasonal demand has resulted in business to the Mid east "booming" said Emirates' cargo manager, Ray Disson, with flights fully booked four to five days in advance with a mix of general cargo on the outbound leg. Cargo from the region includes some produce and fruit --including some from Jordan and Lebanon --, and textiles, largely for the U.S. market.
Cathay Pacific's Gilliard also reported good business to the Middle east, while a forwarder dealing with the region said traffic was picking up.

Johannesburg -- and Cape Town -- remain the key destinations in Africa with markets generally weak elsewhere in the continent. Average rates to Johannesburg are firming, despite additional competition this winter with levels reaching 1.80 stg a kg per 100 kg, possibly against a previous 1.65 a kg.
On the return leg, seasonal fresh produce is in demand to meet Europe's winter demand and this will intensify as the end year holiday season approaches, industry source added.

To Latin America, capacity is tight but rates are steady to Brazil's Sao Paulo at an average of 2.06 stg a kg for 100 kgs. Chemicals and automotive parts are an important part of the traffic to Brazil, with Chile an important destination for machinery.

Enrique Sagra of Iberia which tranships cargo via Maastricht and its Madrid hub said the Spanish carrier had recently out on extra Boeing 747 freighters from Maastricht to try and eliminate the backlog in cargo waiting to be shipped to Latin America.
At the same time, cargo moving through Latin America's key cargo airport -- Miami in Florida -- can be faced with fuel surcharges by some local airlines, a leading cargo agent told Reuters.

Steve Stewart from Lufthansa added that Brazil is probably the strongest South American air cargo market for the UK , but while it is possible to get traffic rights and add extra flights, "there is the problem of trying to find enough cargo to fill the return leg". Trucking is a major competitor to pure airfreight on European routes but Lufthansa has been successful due to its fast overnight "Flash " product to key centres, Stewart added.
"We were concerned at the possible impact of the Channel Tunnel and trucking but the networked "Flash" product via our Frankfurt and Cologne hubs is doing well," he added.

For example, Paris and Brussels are close enough to London to hit by trucking competition, the distances involved and destinations offered by Lufthansa in both eastern Europe and Scandinavia means," we can offer a competitive product with 12 to 24 hour delivery," Stewart said. --Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax +44 171 542 5017
